cognitive_validation.rationale: The old gentleman offers a would-be systematic account (apparatus for observing planetary motion, casting nativities, an observatory), which gestures at an immanent pseudo-scientific logic. But the text treats it as charlatanry and the closing enchantment (a triangle drawn on the forehead transporting Tom) veers toward the magical/supernatural rather than a coherent immanent system, leaving cognitive validation conflicted.

novum_candidates.description: An old gentleman's astrological science that claims to read future events in the stars, cast nativities predicting the precise minute of a person's death, and foretell destined marriages, presented as a functioning predictive apparatus driving the plot.
novum_candidates.estrangement_rationale: The reader is presented with a supposedly infallible stellar prediction that contrasts with the mundane world of lamplighters and watch-houses, but the frame narration and the return-to-start ending dissolve the estrangement into comic tall tale rather than a stably altered world.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The astrological prediction that a destined husband would appear at five o'clock is the engine of the entire central episode: it brings Tom into the house, drives the marriage scheme, the death prediction, and the comic resolution. In terms of plot causation it dominates the narrative, even though the framing undercuts its reality.

novelty.rationale: Astrology and fortune-telling by the stars were part of the contemporary empirical/cultural norm (Francis Moore's almanac is explicitly invoked), not a world-altering totalizing difference. The frame narrator repeatedly undercuts it as pretence, and the ending ('he found himself in the very watch-house') recasts the whole episode as possible enchantment or drunken fantasy rather than a transformed story universe. No estranged world governed by a new astrological law is established.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The story dresses alchemy in pseudo-scientific trappings (crucible, furnace, laboratory instruments, fifteen years of labour, apparatus that explodes), giving a quasi-systematic immanent account, but it is framed comically as charlatanry rather than a coherent working science.

novum_candidates.description: An alchemical laboratory pursuing the philosopher's stone, a substance that turns everything to gold and would make its makers masters of the world, boiling in a crucible that perpetually explodes on the verge of success.
novum_candidates.estrangement_rationale: The alchemical laboratory with its crucible, three-headed child charm, and skeleton offers gothic-scientific estrangement, but the perpetual failure and comic frame prevent it from reshaping the storyworld.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The philosopher's stone is a comic set-piece subordinate to the astrology-driven marriage plot; its explosion is a device to disrupt the wedding rather than the overriding narrative logic. It functions as an incidental (if colourful) backdrop, not the determining engine of the tale.

novelty.rationale: The philosopher's stone never actually functions or transforms the story world; it is perpetually undermined by the running joke that the apparatus always blows up before succeeding. No world-altering difference from the empirical norm is realized, and the frame recasts the episode as fantasy, so no totalizing estranged change is established.

cognitive_validation.rationale: Gas lighting is a coherent, immanent, nonsupernatural technology whose adoption ('the experiment was made, and they lighted up Pall Mall') and economic consequences (obsolescence, calls for compensation) are systematically depicted. It has a consistent cognitive logic as a historical technological development.

novum_candidates.description: The introduction of gas street-lighting, an emergent technology that displaces the old oil-lamp trade and transforms the lamplighters' profession and livelihood.
novum_candidates.estrangement_rationale: The arrival of gas lighting estranges the reader's sense of the lamplighter's craft by rendering an entire trade obsolete, contrasting the romanticized oil-and-cotton past with a mechanized future, but this transformation remains background to the comic tale.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: Although thematically resonant and providing the backdrop for the lamplighters' culture, gas lighting functions as prologue and context for Tom Grig's biography; it does not govern the central astrology/alchemy episode that constitutes the main narrative. It is an incidental (if evocative) framing device rather than the overriding narrative logic.

novelty.rationale: Gas lighting is presented as a genuine technological shift that alters a whole way of life within the story: it is described as the 'death' of the old profession, spelling 'the breaking up of our profession' and the end of the oil-and-cotton trade. This is a real, world-altering change grounded in historical innovation, estranging the lamplighter community's traditional world.
